title: From Good to Great to Built to Last
coreMove: Turn a performance leap into institutional habits that can survive success.
sourcePressure: The source closes by connecting the leap to durability, using disciplined people, disciplined thought, disciplined action, and cumulative momentum as the basis for lasting institutional life without importing detailed Built to Last frameworks.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version treats success as proof the organization is permanently great or turns the ending into a legacy speech.

exampleSpecs.audience: a second-generation foundry president after the firm's best profit year
exampleSpecs.stakes: the leap will decay if quality judgment lives only in the founder's instincts
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the president turns the founder's rejected-casting review into a weekly apprentice ritual instead of announcing a commemorative plaque
exampleSpecs.firstImage: rejected castings cooling on a sand-dusted steel cart

exampleSpecs.domain: public radio newsroom after an investigative award
exampleSpecs.audience: a news director whose team just won its first national prize
exampleSpecs.stakes: the award can either harden standards or become a story the newsroom tells about itself
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director leaves the award unopened until the source-check protocol from the winning series is added to every new investigation kickoff
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a sealed award box beside a stack of marked source logs

exampleSpecs.domain: regional credit union post-growth member discipline
exampleSpecs.audience: a credit union CEO after a merger doubles branch count
exampleSpecs.stakes: growth can dilute the lending discipline that earned member trust
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the CEO compares the merger announcement with three declined loans that protected members, then makes that review part of branch-manager training
exampleSpecs.firstImage: new branch keys lined beside declined-loan summaries

exampleSpecs.audience: an institute director after a breakthrough grant
exampleSpecs.stakes: funding success can silence the debate routines that made the lab worth funding
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director opens the grant meeting by assigning a junior scientist to challenge the flagship hypothesis before any spending plan is approved
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a grant notice projected over a tray of labeled tissue slides

exampleSpecs.audience: a garden director after a popular new conservatory opens
exampleSpecs.stakes: visitor attention could pull resources from the quiet seed-bank discipline that gives the institution its lasting value
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director moves the conservatory ribbon photo below the germination-failure log in the board packet and funds the seed-bank freezer first
exampleSpecs.firstImage: frost crystals on a seed-bank freezer handle

exampleSpecs.domain: children's hospital foundation after a record campaign
exampleSpecs.audience: a foundation president whose campaign exceeded its goal
exampleSpecs.stakes: record donations will not last if stewardship discipline turns into victory-lap events
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the president cancels the gala video montage and instead has fundraisers rehearse the first-year impact review each donor will receive
exampleSpecs.firstImage: unused gala cue cards stacked beside patient-outcome binders

skillTargets: integrate disciplined people, thought, and action without adding unfrozen frameworks
judge whether a victory practice strengthens or weakens institutional life

tryThisNowSpec: Name one recent win. Write the routine, review, or boundary that must exist six months from now for that win to become durable instead of decorative.

sourceAnchors.name: Built to Last
sourceAnchors.detail: the source frames the closing question as whether a good-to-great leap can become durable institutional life rather than a temporary achievement
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Built to Last enters as a harder question: whether the leap can survive the comfort of having made it.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: prevents the timestamp+named-protagonist template from dominating the chapter

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm — a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
